prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: I keep B041 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Six of eight members reach it from theory, materials and spectroscopy backgrounds. The Z2 invariant protected by time-reversal symmetry was a new organising principle, and the HgTe quantum wells gave a measurement I can judge as an experimentalist: edge conductance near 2e^2/h that disappears when the edge is gated off, reproduced by independent groups and probes over fifteen to twenty years. The chain from prediction to first observation is unbroken and can be stated in one citation, which is the main reason I place the quantum spin Hall chain ahead of the broader but less cleanly attributable 3D story. I did not change my configuration since round 1. What round 1 changed is my confidence that the narrow citation is defensible: nobody argued that the Z2 and quantum spin Hall chain is not mature, and the two best objections (Hasan's 3D work, the 2016 prize) concern scope, not validity.
statement.case_against: The credit remains a compromise forced by the three-name limit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state Molenkamp measured, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy built the 3D theory; none can be named, and Zhang's death rules out any later correction. Hasan's ARPES work is a genuine experimental pillar that my configuration leaves out. On the 2016 prize, Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz recognised topological invariants and phase transitions in matter; the Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry, the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation as a helical edge state are new relative to that, but the committee should word the citation so it does not read as a second helping of the same idea. I also accept that choosing B041 in 2026 may defer optical lattice clocks, which is a sequencing cost and not a scientific objection to B013.

responses.point: Danielsson holds Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing that the experimental side deserves two slots and that Hasan's ARPES work made topological insulators a materials class.
responses.response: This is the strongest rival configuration and I take the materials argument seriously. I still cannot support it. It separates Kane from Mele, whose joint Z2 paper and graphene proposal are one theoretical step, and you acknowledge that Mele's role is central. Hasan's 3D result also rests on a theory chain (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Roy) that is only partly inside our names, so crediting the 3D experiment while omitting that theory gives a less clean credit than the 2D chain, where proposal and first observation are directly linked. Since Kane appears in both configurations, the only real difference between us is Mele versus Hasan, and I weigh unbroken attribution of the origin above breadth of materials. If the committee wants the 3D story recognised, I would accept that being argued as a later part and not as a substitution for Mele.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B013 (Katori and Ye) on precision and testability, states that he would not oppose B041, and flags a possible conflict through John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice clock is a strong, cleanly attributed invention, and it is the alternative I rank highest. On the chair's last question, I think breadth and precision are not exclusive criteria here. B041 also has a decisive measurement (quantised edge conductance in HgTe), and what separates the two is that B041 created a classification that reorganised a field, whereas B013 improved an instrument class that is already partly recognised by the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes. Your point that the redefinition of the second has not happened is one I would also not rely on. I welcome the disclosure of your Hall-group connection: given Ye's link to that group, I would have you take part in the scientific discussion of B013 but would not count your preference as independent evidence on Katori and Ye, and I see no need to settle recusal while B041 leads.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and if the committee insists on recognising 3D materials would argue for a second part and not displace Mele.
responses.response: I agree on the configuration and on your proposal as the fallback if the 3D case must be recognised. A second part is attractive in principle but I think it is not available within a three-person cap: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp already use all three slots, so a second part would need Hasan alone and would then sit awkwardly with the Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents theory. For the 2016 prize you left the weight unresolved; my answer is that the Z2 and quantum spin Hall work is new relative to the topological phase transition prize, but the citation should say so in its wording.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B029 to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, stating that omitting Mele was the weaker position, but holds it with only moderate confidence.
responses.response: Thank you for the change; it narrows the committee's disagreement and I agree with your reason. On the chair's question about B029, I treat Xue's quantum anomalous Hall realisation as a later, derived achievement that builds on the topological insulator concept and magnetic doping, so it belongs in neither this citation nor a rival ballot. Treating B029 as the same story would, however, make the citation too broad to attribute, and I would keep the wording to the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification to avoid being drawn into that overlap.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B013 and argues that clocks have a cleaner attribution than any three-person B041 configuration, because the choice between Mele and Hasan is not made by the evidence.
responses.response: I accept that the clock attribution is cleaner, and I do not call B013 wrong. But in B041 the choice of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp follows a clear logic: the two authors of the Z2 theory and the experimenter who first observed the state. What the evidence leaves unresolved is who else deserves recognition, not who these three are. I also agree with Mehlig that the Hasan question is one of scope and not of the experimental fingerprint, and I would not count the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as a reason for B013, because every candidate on the shortlist leaves out contributors somewhere.

uncertainties: Whether Mele or Hasan is the better third name; I hold Mele with moderate confidence and accept that it remains a judgment about attribution, not physics merit.
How to word the citation so it neither implies that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang or Fu, Moore and Balents are credited, nor overstates priority.
How much of the Z2 and quantum spin Hall work the committee regards as new relative to the 2016 prize, which I judge to be substantial but not unanimous.
My recollection of the 2D and 3D priority chronology is unverified, and whether choosing B041 now defers B013 to a later year cannot be known.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I have no recorded tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or the B018 candidates. My connections are to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur and KTH astroparticle physics. B016 (IceCube) lies in a neighbouring field, which I would note if it came into contention, but it is not part of my configuration. I note Kroll's possible link to B013 through the Hall group and have not found it to disqualify B041.
